checks.finding: A turn's lease waits for a pending reconnect, and a reconnect never closes a leased runtime (fixed; was: a turn admitted while the provider looked connected leased the runtime a pending reconnect registered, and cancelling that reconnect closed it under the turn).
Removing a provider drops its pending reconnect as it enters removal_pending (fixed; was: the reconnect outlived the removal).
Every pending attempt keeps an owner, including when the renderer is destroyed before binding (fixed; BRW-005).

Leases are refused once close() begins, and a runtime that finishes starting after it is closed again (fixed; was: a turn admitted before shutdown created and registered a runtime after the maps were cleared).

The default family is live, or P's managed family while P is active, as after a no-eligible refresh whether P stays connected or disconnects (decided; PROV-008 Q15). The enabled choice and the recovery cause are checked by the Rust tests, not this model.

One launch per reservation; stop reports what the graph holds; terminal states are absorbing; an admitted child's provider runs under held access, which the host releases once the run ends; its attempt ends, and its lease record is released, only after it settles and its provider run ends.

With observations that no longer time out, a child whose provider is still running is never failed for it (fixed; was: the 5 s control timeout failed running children). The re-poll itself is proved by provider_end_waits_through_observation_timeouts, not by this check.
A failed activation fails the child in both stores through the launch-failure cleanup (fixed; was: it settled the execution row while the graph current stayed active).
Without the fix, a failed activation settles the execution row while the graph current stays active.
A child whose provider exits cleanly without Return is failed and settles (fixed; was: it never settled, and with admission its attempt and leases were held forever).
Without the clean-exit check, a child whose provider exits cleanly without Return never settles.
Start-failure cleanup fails the current with a reason the graph accepts (fixed; was: retried a rejected reason forever).
Start-failure cleanup settles a current another actor already terminated, with that current's outcome (fixed; was: retried forever).
Without child admission, a selected child's provider runs with no held lease or attempt (the behavior before child admission).
Restart reconciliation does not abort on a state the product produced.
The candidate fixes restore every safety invariant.
With the candidate fixes, every claimed child settles and releases its lease record and provider access.

With every fault on, a leased runtime stays open, no runtime closes under a running turn, a turn runs only under held access, access is never released while its turn runs, no host timer targets a running turn's access, only a cancelled turn is ever force-stopped, and the app always starts.

With no faults, every safety invariant holds, every lease is released, every lease debt is reconciled, every attempt whose turn ended stops holding the provider, and a removal completes without a restart.

Rust giving up on a running turn and then releasing its lease cancels the turn; the access is released only when the native turn ends (fixed; was: released under the live turn, so removal could close the runtime under it).
Without the host owning the release, Rust's release after it gave up frees the access under the live native turn, and removal then closes the runtime under it.
An admission whose release was decided cannot be claimed, so a timer release never lands under a running turn (fixed; was: the 30 s admission timer's release completed after the claim).
Without the claim check, a claim during an in-flight admission release runs the turn, and the release then frees its access.

A failed admission release still blocks the claim, because releaseRequested is sticky (fixed; was: the claim succeeded and the turn ran with no counted lease). A2's fix is off here: a refused finalize is the only modeled way a release fails.
A removal completes without a restart even though the host releases the last lease before Rust ends the attempt: the owner's acknowledgement retries the refused finalize (fixed; A2).
Without the acknowledgement retry, the finalize refused while the attempt still ran is never retried, and removal waits for a restart.
Without the unknown-release retry, access released before the owner's release is forgotten after ten minutes; the owner's later release finds nothing to acknowledge, and removal waits for a restart.
Settling a quarantined attempt, from the thread view or an action destination, wakes the lease reconciler, so its lease debt is reconciled (fixed; D; was: debt left until restart).
Without the wake, a settled quarantined attempt's lease debt waits for a restart. C's fix is off here: it releases the lease when the native run ends, so the settle would leave no debt.
A turn whose terminal state cannot be persisted still releases its access, because the host releases it when the native turn ends (fixed; C lease half; was: held forever).
Without the host owning the release, a turn whose terminal state cannot be persisted holds its lease forever. C's attempt fix is off here: it would release the lease from the product side.
A startup that finds a removal_pending provider whose quarantined attempt still runs now starts, leaving the provider removal_pending (fixed; E's startup failure).
Without it, the refused finalize in reconcileStartup fails every startup. E's removal fix is off here: it stops the quarantined attempt from counting, so the finalize would not be refused.
An attempt left running by a failed persist under a removal no longer fails startup (fixed; E via C).

A removal that waited on a turn finishes at the next start even when startup quarantines that turn's submitted input: its attempt ran in the process that exited, so startup records its native-run end and the drain no longer counts it (fixed; E removal half).

Without it, the quarantined attempt still counts as running after the restart, so the removal stays pending until its thread is opened (the unknown-release retry then finishes it) or the app restarts again.

After a restart, once the quarantined attempt becomes terminal, the owner's release of a lease the fresh host does not know retries every drained removal, so the removal finishes in-session. E's restart fix is off here: with it, startup's own finalize succeeds and this retry is never needed.

A turn whose terminal state cannot be persisted stops holding the provider once its native run ends: its attempt stays undecided for reconciliation, its lease is released, and the drain no longer counts it (fixed; C attempt half).
Without it, a turn whose terminal state cannot be persisted leaves its attempt running, which blocks the provider tombstone until a restart.

A cancelled turn that ignored the cancellation and was force-stopped also stops holding the provider: its attempt ends even when its terminal state cannot be persisted. The turn is cancelled by Rust giving up or by the user's Stop.
Without C's attempt fix, a force-stopped turn whose terminal state cannot be persisted leaves its attempt running, so it keeps holding the provider.
A removal waiting on a turn whose terminal state cannot be persisted finishes without a restart, and the ended attempt's lease is reconciled once (fixed; C).
Without it, that removal waits for a restart.
A pending removal whose finalize or cleanup fails at startup for another reason is recorded and left for the next start; the app still starts (fixed; L6).
Without isolation, that failure rejects reconcileStartup and Relayer cannot start.
A cancelled native turn that ignores the cancellation is force-stopped after two minutes, and its access is then released (fixed; G; was: it kept its provider access forever).
Without the per-turn force-stop, a cancelled native turn that ignores the cancellation keeps its provider access forever.

Startup restores ready only from the app server's own record for the same digest when the runtime files validate, so a withdrawn route stays withdrawn (fixed R1; was: restart restored a ready the JSON catalog still held after Rust recorded unavailable).
With the JSON catalog as a second record, a crash between the Rust and JSON writes restores a ready that Rust had withdrawn, and Send is admitted on it (R1, the behavior before the fix).
There is one readiness record, so no failed write can split it (fixed R2; was: a failed JSON write left the two stores disagreeing with no reconciliation).
With two records, a JSON write that fails after the Rust commit leaves them disagreeing (R2, the behavior before the fix).
Rust rejects a generation older than one it accepted in the same process, so an older result never replaces a newer one, even when a request outlives its client (fixed R3).
Without the generation guard, a request that reaches Rust after its client gave up replaces a newer result (R3 mechanism; plausible: needs a request that outlives its client).
The latest evaluation always reaches the app server.

Choosing a default provider also selects its managed family, so no later refresh changes the chosen provider or family (fixed, PROV-008; was: the next refresh of the family's provider moved the default provider back to it).
From an unset default family, a refresh may fill the family with its provider, but once the user chooses a provider and family no refresh changes them (PROV-008).
Without the pairing, the Settings provider choice stores only the provider, and the next refresh of the default family's provider moves the default provider back to it.

A refresh that discovered before a reconnect carries the older connection generation, so its stale result has no effect (fixed, PROV-002; was: it published over the reconnect and nothing queued behind it corrected that).
Without the connection generation, a refresh that discovered before a reconnect publishes its stale disconnected result after the reconnect, and nothing queued behind it corrects that.
An eligible result discovered before a zero-eligible reconnect carries the older generation and cannot reactivate the tombstoned family (fixed, PROV-002).
Without the connection generation, an eligible result discovered before a reconnect that found zero eligible models reactivates the tombstoned managed family.

A refresh resolves its adapter when it runs, so a refresh queued before a reconnect runs through the reconnect's runtime (fixed, PROV-002; was: it ran through the captured unavailable stub and contradicted the reconnect).
Without run-time resolution, a refresh captures its adapter when requested; the unavailable stub it captured publishes after a reconnect replaced it and contradicts the reconnect.
Logout commits its signed-out state with the next generation and no longer waits inside the provider queue for its refresh, so it returns (fixed, CR-V7).
Logout waits inside the provider queue for its own refresh, which is queued behind an explicit stub recovery that waits for the provider queue: neither returns.

A cancelled reconnect leaves the active provider a catalog adapter: a fresh runtime, or the recovery adapter when none can start. With the real adapter, a tombstoned default family restores once the provider is healthy (fixed, F4/V8).
A cancelled reconnect unregisters the catalog adapter of an active provider, so no refresh can run for it and a tombstoned default family never restores.

Connect registers the catalog adapter only after the definition commits, so nothing refreshes or publishes for a provider that does not exist yet (fixed, PROV-007; was: the adapter was registered before the commit).
Registering the catalog adapter before the commit gives a provider an adapter before its definition exists.

With every fix, a settled execution row has a terminal current and product row, and startup leaves no interrupted child active. The user can send whenever no message turn runs, two message turns never run at once, a run the user invokes never waits, and the product neither stops nor runs an agent's child.
Without a restart, every child the parent launched ends in the graph, and its product row ends once its parent is done.
Across up to two restarts, every child the product recorded ends in the graph and in the product.

Known open: a crash after the parent's prepareComplete but before the broker's first product write leaves a graph-only child whose current stays active; no product row names it, so startup cannot fail it.
Without the activation fix, a failed activation settles the execution row while the current stays active and the product row stays submitted.
Without the activation fix, an awaiting parent never sees the child end: nothing runs it, and a retry answers 200 with no launch.
Without the startup fix, a restart between the child row and `launching` re-binds the child but leaves its current active.
Without the refused-launch cleanup, an ambiguous preparation leaves the claimed child submitted and unbound with its current active.
Without the refused-launch cleanup, the claimed child's product row stays submitted after its parent is done, so its turn never ends.
Before the decision, a child that still runs after its parent is done refuses the user's next message (the gate counted it as a turn).
Before the decision (#717), the gate counted a user's invoked run as the thread's one active turn: an invoke waited for the running message turn, and the next message waited for the invoke.
Before the decision, the product accepted a Stop for an agent's child, and a user's invoke of the delegate action ran the child on the product path.
A catalog publish changes only its own provider's managed family and never a custom family.
A default family tombstoned by a zero-eligible refresh stays the default and blocks Send.
A tombstoned default family restores once its provider is healthy and its real adapter is registered.
Text typed while a follow-up is in flight survives the new turn loading (fixed; #512: it stayed in the old turn's draft scope, which was never shown again).
The same holds when the prompt was re-enabled by leaving the thread and returning during the POST (fixed; #512).
Settlement clears only text the send carried (fixed; #513: re-entering a scope could repeat a revision, so a successful send cleared and deleted text typed after Send).
A settled send does not leave its text in the composer (fixed; #513: re-entering a scope during a send bumped its revision without a text change, so settlement kept the sent text).
At most one follow-up per thread is in flight, and every send releases its thread's Send button.
Moving unsent text to the newest turn's scope and keeping a scope's revision unless its text changes restore every composer promise.

Input made while an annotation draft resolves waits and the latest proceeds (fixed; #514), the selection is re-rendered from the latest state once the draft resolves (fixed; #515), and a drafted node reopens its editor (PRD L2203).
Without superseding it, a switch waiting on a draft save commits its node, reporting it and recording it in history, before a click queued meanwhile replaces it (review of #514).
Send waits for an authored input commit started by the click, so it carries the answer and is not refused (fixed; #521: the Send could go without the answer, or be refused by it).
Without the wait, a Send served before the commit goes without the answer (#521).
Without keeping a failed commit, one that fails before the click is forgotten, and the Send goes without the answer (review of #521).
Without moving unsent text into the newest turn's scope, text typed during a send is stranded (#512).

With turns created elsewhere in the thread (an authored invoke) arriving while Send waits for an input commit, the composer keeps its promises (fixed in review of #512: the text was carried into the newer turn and stayed after it was sent).
Without holding the submission from the click, a newer turn that arrives while Send waits for an input commit carries the text it then sends, and the text stays after the send (review of #512).
Without holding a send that may have been sent, its text is carried into the turn it created and can be sent again (review of #512; SCP-019).
Without retiring it, stranded text the user replaced by typing stays in its scope and is carried forward once the prompt empties (review of #512, SCP-021).
Without handing it back, the text of a send lost to a network or server error stays stranded in its scope when an unrelated turn arrived while it was pending (review of #512, SCP-019).
Without waiting, input made while a draft resolves is dropped (#514).
Without the refresh, a refused switch can leave the kept node's detail disposed (#515).

A dragged node follows the pointer and stays where it is left across renders and view round trips, and only a pan or a new layout moves the camera (fixed; #531: a render during a drag froze the node).
Without re-binding, a render during a drag leaves the drag on the replaced node, which stops following the pointer (#531).
Without the fit after the drop, a layout that changed mid-drag is never fitted, and new nodes can stay off-screen (review of #531).
Without fitting before the view is cached, leaving mid-drag after a layout change caches the unfitted camera, and returning restores it (review of #531).

A root turn never fails on a thread Codex cannot resume, never resumes a killed conversation, keeps resuming across providers that share a Codex home, and reports every reset (fixed; was: a provider switch or a Stop before turn/start pinned an unresumable thread, and every later root turn failed with "no rollout found", even across restart).
Without a recorded binding, a follow-up in another Codex home resumes a thread that has no rollout there.
Saving the thread when thread/start answers, not when turn/start is accepted, pins a thread a Stop left without a rollout.
Without the missing-rollout recovery, a thread saved by an earlier release that has no rollout in the turn's home fails the root turn.
If a force-stop or force shutdown keeps the saved thread, the next root turn resumes the conversation the killed turn may have left mid-write.
If onTurnId saves a thread whose turn/start answer arrives after the force, the forced conversation is saved again and resumed.
If a force before turn/start also forgets the saved thread, the next root turn starts fresh although nothing wrote the thread.
Binding the thread to its provider definition instead of its Codex home drops native history when a follow-up moves between API-key providers that share Codex's default home (#584).
If a Stop that kills the app-server while turn/start is pending keeps the saved thread, the next root turn resumes a conversation the kill may have left mid-write.
Without the reset notice, a root turn silently starts a fresh thread after the previous native conversation was lost (#584).
Witness: a root turn really resumes a saved thread, so the resume properties are not vacuous.
Root turns stay serialized, no chained acquisition starts, and two root natives never share a session, with close, force close and crashes.
While the harness is live it never pins or resumes a force-stopped root conversation.
No state the host captures after a force-stop names the stopped session (fixed; was: a graceful close captured the state, a force-stop then fired, and the close persisted the stale capture).
Without recording at the force-stop, a close that captured before the force persists the stopped session.
After a graceful close and restart, the restored session is never a force-stopped conversation (fixed).
Without recording at the force-stop, a turn force-stopped after close persisted is restored after the restart.

Quitting while a root turn runs (force close) does not leave the killed conversation resumable after the restart, and an idle root session, or one a root turn is still acquiring, is kept (fixed; was: force shutdown kept the root session and nothing persisted the change).
If force shutdown keeps the root session, force close persists the killed conversation and the restart resumes it.
If force close does not persist, the previously saved killed conversation is resumed after the restart.
If force shutdown forgets the root session whenever a root turn is in flight, a force close during that turn's session acquisition forgets a session nothing ran on.
Witness: an idle root session survives a force close and the restart, so NoNeedlessForget is not vacuous.
Open, narrowed: a crash after a per-turn force-stop but before its state write lands restores the stopped conversation. The write now starts when the force fires rather than when the host run ends.
A running root turn's session carries its own pinned version's presentation instructions (fixed; was: a rotated session was built from the shared loader's stale cache, PPG-003).
With one shared loader cache that only reload() refreshes, a rotated root session runs with the previous version's instructions.
A force-stopped root turn's host run always ends and frees the session lock, even when its native turn never settles.
A running Codex turn always finds its provider key file, the user count is exact, and no key file remains once every turn ends, with force-stops and a host that stops waiting.
The key file is eventually removed for good.
A turn's lease waits for a pending reconnect, so settling that reconnect never closes or wipes the runtime a turn uses (PROV-004), with every publish fault on.
The acquire guard alone keeps PROV-004: with CancelSparesLease off, no lease exists while a reconnect is pending.
The cancel guard alone also keeps PROV-004: with LeaseWaitsForReconnect off, a settling reconnect spares the runtime a lease holds.
With both lease fixes off, a turn leases the runtime a pending reconnect is signing in, and cancelling the reconnect closes it and wipes its home under the turn.
Leases are refused once close() begins, and a runtime that finishes starting after it is closed again.
With ShutdownRefusesLeases off, a lease queued before shutdown registers a runtime after close() cleared the maps, and nothing closes it.
No refresh starts or publishes during a pending reconnect, so an automatic result never stands for the reconnect's sign-in, and Rust never reads P ready with no login.
With RefreshSkipsPendingReconnect off, a refresh publishes ready through the runtime a reconnect is signing in, before the user's reconnect settles.
A reconnect whose answer was lost is adopted when the generation reads back advanced, and keeps its login when the read fails too.
With LostReconnectAdopted and CancelSignsOut off (the code before this fix), a reconnect the app server committed settles as failed and its cancel wipes the login the app server reads as connected.

An unanswered reconnect is adopted only when the app server committed it, including after a sign-out during the reconnect, a baseline read that failed, and an earlier sign-out request that commits late.
With AdoptChecksBaseline off, any advance past the reconnect's baseline is adopted: a sign-out during the reconnect supersedes it, the refusal's answer is lost, and the refused reconnect is adopted.

With AdoptTracksLostWrites off, a sign-out whose answer was lost commits only after the next reconnect read its baseline; the reconnect's refused publish loses its answer too, reads one step past the baseline, and is adopted.
A reconnect the app server committed is never settled and wiped, with every fault on, including a sign-out during the reconnect whose publish got no answer.
With LostReconnectAdopted off, a reconnect whose committed publish lost its answer is settled and its login wiped.
A settled reconnect never leaves the app server reading ready over the login it wiped: it commits signed-out first, and keeps the login when that publish fails, with every fault on.
With CancelSignsOut off, a sign-out whose publish failed leaves Rust ready; a reconnect then starts and is cancelled, wiping the login while Rust still reads ready.
With CancelKeepsUnrecordedLogin off, a cancel whose signed-out publish fails still wipes the login, while a failed sign-out left the app server reading ready.
Once the app server answered a sign-out, the home holds no login again until the user starts a new reconnect, with every fault on.

With SupersededCancelWipes off, a sign-out answered during a reconnect is followed by the browser sign-in; the refused reconnect's settle cannot publish, keeps the new login, and the next refresh would publish connected over the confirmed sign-out.
No provider access is granted while P has no login and the app server still reads it ready, with every fault on, including a cancel after a sign-out whose publish failed.
With SignOutBlocksAdmission off, a sign-out whose publish fails leaves the app server ready, and a turn takes provider access with no login.
A refresh that resolved its generation before a reconnect and read the account mid-sign-in is dropped after the reconnect is cancelled, because the cancel advanced the generation.
With CancelSignsOut off, a refresh straddling a cancelled reconnect passes both generation checks and publishes ready over the wiped login.

A refresh that overlapped a reconnect never readies the app server over a wiped login, including when the cancel's own publish fails: every path that wipes first advances the generation, and a cancel that cannot keeps the login. The sign-out fault is off; its own straddle is the known limit.
With CancelKeepsUnrecordedLogin off, a cancel whose signed-out publish fails wipes the login without advancing the generation, and a refresh that straddled the reconnect publishes ready over it.
PROV-003: a removal that waited on the turn finishes once the turn releases, with every fault on.
Preparation reuses an installation only when it passes startup's full validation, so readiness is never published for an installation the next start rejects (fixed R1).

When reuse checks only that the entrypoints execute, a Repair after the private state, ownership marker or entrypoint confinement broke publishes ready for an installation startup rejects (R1, the behavior before the fix).
A route an evaluation made ready survives a restart that changes neither digest nor recipe (fixed R1).
Before the fix, Repair republished ready on a broken layout, and the next unchanged restart dropped it again, so Repair never stuck (R1).
With both fixes, startup still restores only from the app server's record (PROV-006), the latest evaluation still wins (PROV-005), and a route marked due is never ready, across two restarts.
The same holds from a row an older build left ready, which migration 0034 verifies again once.

An upgrade that changes the digest gets one committed evaluation without a Repair, also when the app restarts before it commits (fixed #556). The model assumes a connected provider publishes a route; without one the mark waits.
Without the automatic evaluation, a changed digest leaves both providers pending until someone presses Repair (#556, the behavior before the fix).
A route restores ready only when an evaluation measured it on the recipe the release requires, so an upgrade that changes only the recipe starts pending (fixed, PR #576 review).
Without the recorded recipe, an upgrade whose staged runtime activated restores the ready measured on the old recipe, with the same digest, and Send uses a runtime no evaluation checked.
Without the recorded recipe, an upgrade that changes only the recipe, for example one whose activation failed, is never marked due and waits for Repair.
Every started evaluation, automatic or not, settles.
Witness, not a bug: readiness is per harness, so an evaluation not started for a provider (another provider's Repair, or the automatic one) makes its shared route ready too.
